claim: Sierra built its own Kubernetes-native agent sandbox orchestration layer (Agency) rather than use an off-the-shelf sandbox provider because the agent-sandbox problem space was too undefined to inherit someone else's trade-offs.
stance_target: custom cloud sandbox infrastructure for autonomous coding agents is preferable to off-the-shelf providers when resource/time/concurrency limits are hard constraints
scope_conditions: Sierra's internal employee agent (Pinecone) and customer-facing agent-builder (Ghostwriter), 2026
quoted_support: When the problem is not yet clearly defined, or it's not clear which trade-offs are right, you inherit someone else's assumptions and spend your time working around them instead of understanding your own problem. So we decided to build our own.

claim: Agents given full unrestricted access tokens (sandbox_mode = 'danger-full-access') pose unacceptable risk because the agent inherits the developer's write access to systems too dangerous for unattended autonomous operation.
stance_target: autonomous coding agents require scoped, non-root, credential-isolated sandboxes rather than full developer permissions
scope_conditions: Sierra's prototype agent deployments before Agency existed
quoted_support: Running the agent with --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions or sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" was not really an option. That would mean that the agent would run with the developer's access token, which had write access to systems that were too dangerous to give to an agent, especially an unattended one.

claim: Sierra observed a 2-4 order-of-magnitude difference between the number of active runner instances in the last 8 hours versus the last 8 days, because unattended agents spend most of their time idle waiting for input.
stance_target: autonomous agent infrastructure must assume idle-dominant utilization and build auto-hibernation of idle agents
quoted_support: There is usually 2 to 4 orders of magnitude difference between the number of active runner instances within the last 8 hours compared to the last 8 days.

claim: Agency decouples runner and application communication via async input/output message queues (Elasticache Redis Streams) with checkpoint-based finite-state-machine replay, achieving p50 8ms / p99 40ms round trips, enabling transparent hibernation and resume of idle agent sandboxes.
stance_target: message-queue-decoupled FSM checkpointing is a viable mechanism for cost-efficient idle-agent hibernation at scale
quoted_support: By using an in-memory queue implementation, like Elasticache Redis Streams, and limiting the size of the events (a few hundred KiB) we can make the round trips fast enough (p50: 8ms, p99: 40ms) when both parties are online.

claim: All LLM inference within Sierra's agent runners is routed through an external proxy outside the sandbox so real API keys are never exposed to the agent, preventing exfiltration by a jailbroken agent.
stance_target: agents should never hold direct API keys/secrets; credential injection must happen at a proxy layer outside agent reach
quoted_support: All inference in runners happens via an LLM proxy, running outside of the sandbox. This allows us to inject real api keys just in time and also do token accounting without cooperation or potential meddling by a compromised agent.

claim: Owning the full agentic stack (orchestration, sandboxing, MCP gateway, UX) allowed Sierra to ship a customer-data-isolated 'Ephemeral Sessions' feature in under a week, an velocity advantage attributed to not being blocked by a third-party vendor.
stance_target: vertically-integrated, in-house agent infrastructure accelerates feature delivery versus dependence on third-party sandbox vendors
quoted_support: we were able to build “Ephemeral Sessions” in Pinecone in under a week. These sessions are the only ones in which customer data is allowed to be loaded
